volumes.title: In Reply to Yours
volumes.text:
Emberwick Post Office, the ninth of October. To Mr Aldous Crake, Inspector of Rural Offices, District Postal Board, Lowmarket. Sir, I have your notice. It informs me that this office is under review and may be replaced by a wall box, emptied twice weekly by the Lowmarket carrier. Your reason is that Emberwick handles forty-one letters a week, and the Board requires one hundred.

I have been postmistress here nineteen years and have never handled so few as forty-one letters, not even the week of the flood. I do not say your figure is wrong. I say that I should like to meet whoever counted it.

A wall box cannot sell a stamp, Mr Crake, nor tell a boy that his sevens look like ones. I shall count for myself, beginning Monday, and you shall have my figures. I remain, with respect and some surprise, Winifred Tansy, Postmistress.

volumes.title: A Week Properly Counted
volumes.text:
To Mr Crake, Inspector of Rural Offices, Lowmarket, from Winifred Tansy, Postmistress at Emberwick, whose office your Board proposes to close for want of letters. Sir, I promised you figures and here they are.

I counted every item that crossed this counter from Monday to Saturday. I used dried peas, one into a jar for each letter, because a pea cannot be argued with afterwards. The total is two hundred and twelve letters, nine parcels, and a hat-box for Mrs Peabody, which I have counted as a parcel though it behaved like furniture.

Your figure was forty-one. Mine is two hundred and twelve. One of us has mislaid one hundred and seventy-one letters a week, and I have looked under my counter. The jar is on the shelf should you wish to inspect the peas. I have not eaten any. Yours faithfully, W. Tansy.

volumes.title: What a Wall Box Cannot
volumes.text:
To Mr Crake, Inspector of Rural Offices, Lowmarket, from the Postmistress at Emberwick. Sir, since your Board weighs this office against a wall box, permit me to list what crossed my counter on Thursday that was not a letter.

Old Silas Fenn came in with a letter from his daughter in the Lowlands. His eyes are gone, so I read it to him twice by the stove, the second time slower for the part about the baby. Mrs Peabody collected the spare key to number nine, which I keep with thirteen others on a board behind the scales. A drover asked the road to Stonecrop. A small girl asked how to spell sincerely and was told.

None of this earned the Board a penny. I mention it because your form has no line for it, and I thought you should know what the line would say. Yours faithfully, Winifred Tansy.

volumes.title: Concerning the Half-Ounce
volumes.text:
Emberwick Post Office, to Mr Crake, Inspector, at the District Postal Board. Sir, I have your reply of two lines, which says my figures are noted. I have noted that they are noted.

Since an inspection may follow, I had better confess something before you find it. The brass letter scale on my counter lacks its half-ounce weight. It rolled between the floorboards eleven years ago and is there still; I hear it when the carrier stamps his boots. In its place I use a horn button from a drover’s coat. I have tested that button against the Lowmarket weights and it is true to a hair.

Every letter in Emberwick has been weighed honestly against it. I should rather you heard this from me than discovered it and supposed the rest of the office ran on buttons. Yours faithfully, Winifred Tansy, Postmistress.

volumes.title: An Invitation, With Directions
volumes.text:
To Mr Aldous Crake, Inspector of Rural Offices, Lowmarket. Sir, I have now written you four letters about whether Emberwick should keep its post office, and I believe you have never seen it. I write to invite you.

Take the branch train to Emberwick and walk down Ember Street as far as the pump. The office is the one with the red door, which wants painting; I say so before you do. Come on a Tuesday if you can. Tuesday is when the Fell bag and the Marsh bag go out, and the bench by the stove is full by three.

You need not announce yourself. I would sooner you saw the place as it is than as it looks with the brass polished. There will be tea at four in either case, as there is every day, Board or no Board. Yours faithfully, Winifred Tansy, Postmistress.

volumes.title: Two Sealed Bags
volumes.text:
Emberwick Post Office, the second of December. To Mr Crake, Inspector, Lowmarket. Sir, I have found your missing letters, and they were never lost. Your Board says this office handles forty-one letters a week. My own count is two hundred and twelve.

I asked Barnaby Sedge, the carrier, who has more sense than he lets on. Every letter for the Northern Fells goes from here in one sealed bag, and every letter for the marsh in another. Neither is opened until Lowmarket, where the letters are stamped and counted to Lowmarket’s credit. One hundred and seventy-one a week, Mr Crake. I sort them, bag them and seal them, and your clerk counts them as his own.

What remains is Emberwick writing to Emberwick: forty-one. I do not blame the clerk. I only ask that somebody open the bags on paper as well as in fact. Yours, W. Tansy.

volumes.title: Snow on the Fell Road
volumes.text:
To Mr Crake, Inspector of Rural Offices, from Winifred Tansy, Postmistress at Emberwick, the office your Board thinks of replacing with a box on a wall. Sir, this is to report the week of the snow.

On Tuesday the carrier’s cart could not climb past the second milestone. The Fell bag held forty letters, among them a doctor’s note for Stonecrop and a seed catalogue somebody has waited on since autumn. I put on my brother’s boots and carried it up myself, four miles, to the Drover’s Rest, where the shepherds collect. Tom Pellow, my post boy, minded the counter and sold nine stamps without me.

I do not tell you this to be admired. My feet have had the admiring of it. I tell you because a wall box would have spent that Tuesday under a drift, keeping its letters dry and to itself. Yours faithfully, W. Tansy.

volumes.title: The Gentleman With the Umbrella
volumes.text:
Emberwick Post Office, a Thursday in February. To Mr Aldous Crake, Inspector of Rural Offices. Sir, the stationmaster tells me that the gentleman who sheltered here from the rain on Tuesday, and stayed an hour, was yourself.

Then you have seen the office after all. You sat on the bench by the stove between Silas Fenn and the coal scuttle. You heard me read Mr Fenn his daughter’s letter. You held Mrs Peabody’s wool while she wound it, which was good of you, since she asks everybody and most find they are in a hurry. You carried the Fell bag out to the carrier’s cart without being asked, and you drank two cups of tea.

Had I known, I should have used the good cups. On reflection I am glad I did not know. You saw a Tuesday, sir, and that was all I wanted. Yours faithfully, Winifred Tansy, Postmistress.

volumes.title: One Umbrella, Returned
volumes.text:
To Mr Crake, Inspector of Rural Offices, Lowmarket, from the Postmistress at Emberwick. Sir, you left a brown umbrella under my bench the wet Tuesday you called. I return it by this post. It would not sit on the scale, so I have charged it as a walking stick and paid the postage myself.

I thank you for your letter, which ran to four pages where its predecessors ran to two lines. You ask questions no form of the Board’s has asked me in nineteen years, and I answer them gladly. I keep fourteen spare keys. I read letters aloud to three people and write them for two. Mothers have weighed five babies on the parcel scale this winter; all were found satisfactory.

You ask last whether I would mind your putting such things before the Board. I would mind very much if you did not. Yours faithfully, Winifred Tansy.

volumes.title: A Petition, Unrequested
volumes.text:
Emberwick Post Office, the first week of March. To Mr Aldous Crake, Inspector, District Postal Board. Sir, you write that the Board meets on the twentieth to decide whether this office stays open. I enclose something I did not ask for and cannot in conscience withhold.

Mrs Peabody has got up a petition. It carries ninety-six signatures, eleven crosses duly witnessed, and one paw print, which belongs to the baker’s dog and which I have asked her to explain. She says he comes in every day and has a right to an opinion. Old Mr Fenn signed by feel. The schoolchildren signed in a column, getting larger toward the bottom.

I told her that boards are moved by figures and not by feelings. She said, then count the names, that is a figure. I had no answer, sir, so I send it to you. Yours faithfully, Winifred Tansy, Postmistress.

volumes.title: An Ordinary Day, Set Down
volumes.text:
To Mr Crake, Inspector of Rural Offices, from Winifred Tansy, Postmistress at Emberwick. Sir, the Board met yesterday and I shall not hear its decision for a week. Nothing in this letter needs an answer. I only wish one ordinary day to be on record, whichever way it has gone.

I unlocked at seven. Tom Pellow swept the step. I sold thirty stamps, weighed one goose in a basket, and sorted the Fell bag while the kettle boiled. At three the bench filled. At four there was tea. At six I emptied the box in the wall, and the shutter gave the small clap it has given every evening for nineteen years.

Then I lit the lamp in the window, as I always do, so the carrier can find the door in the dark. It is burning as I write. Yours faithfully, W. Tansy.

volumes.title: The Board Decides
volumes.text:
Emberwick Post Office, the last day of March. To Mr Aldous Crake, Inspector. Sir, your letter came by the morning cart and I read it standing up. The office is to stay. The Fell bag and the Marsh bag are to be counted to Emberwick, all two hundred and twelve letters of us, and the wall box is to go to some village that has asked for one.

I thank the Board for the parcel also. The new half-ounce weight sits on the scale as though it had never been away. The horn button has retired to the shelf beside my jar of peas, with honour. Tom Pellow is painting the door with your tin of red paint, and a good deal of himself.

Your umbrella being home, you will want a fresh excuse to call. I suggest tea. Four o’clock, any Tuesday. Yours sincerely, Winifred Tansy, Postmistress.

volumes.title: Behind the Churchyard Wall
volumes.text:
Dear Arlo, you went on the carrier’s cart yesterday at eight. I know it was eight because I was behind the churchyard wall and heard the clock. I saw your mother holding the birdcage and your father counting boxes. I saw you look round at the pump twice. I did not come out.

I am not sending this. I am writing it because Mam says a thing written down stops going round your head. So far she is wrong.

The day before, at the weir, I said you pushed the Otter off early, and then I said, good, go to Loam End then. I have still got your brass compass in my pocket. The needle sticks at north-east the same as ever. This letter is going in the toffee tin in the hollow willow, where nobody goes but us. Jem Aldery.

volumes.title: Conkers and Your Desk
volumes.text:
Dear Arlo, it is October and you have been at Loam End a month. I am not posting this one either. It is going in the toffee tin in our willow by the weir, on top of the first.

The big chestnut by the forge has dropped everything at once. I have a conker that has beaten nine others, and nobody to tell who would understand how much that is. You would have soaked yours in vinegar and said you hadn’t.

They have put a new boy at your desk. His name is Wilf Dabb, he comes from the marsh, and he keeps his pencils in a row. Your initials are still cut under the lid, where Mr Greave has never found them. I looked. I have not said one word to Wilf about them, or about you. I still have your compass. Jem.

volumes.title: The Dam Goes Out
volumes.text:
Dear Arlo, this is the third letter I have written since you moved to the Lowlands, and the third I am not sending. They live in a tin in the hollow willow. You would know the tin. It was your toffee.

The Ember came up on Sunday night, brown and loud, over the stepping stones. Our dam went. All of it: the flat stone you carried from the ford, the clay we packed in with our heels, the stick with the flag. It took us all August, and the river took it in one night without noticing.

In the morning the willow was standing in water to its knees but the tin was dry on its ledge. I thought you would want to know about the dam. Then I remembered what I said to you at the weir, and I did not know what you would want. Jem.

volumes.title: The Sledge Steers Left
volumes.text:
Dear Arlo, there is snow on Kiln Hill, and I took the Bathtub up by myself. I am telling you in a letter I shall not post. It goes in the tin in our willow with the others, because of what I said the day before you left for Loam End.

The sledge we built steers left now. It never did with two. I think you were the weight that kept it straight, sitting behind with your boots dug in. I went into the hedge four times. The Pellow twins laughed, and I said the runner was bent, which it is not.

On the fifth go I sat further back, where you sat, and it ran true all the way to the gate. So that is how it is done. I walked home with the rope over my shoulder and nobody to take a turn pulling. Jem.

volumes.title: Where the Needle Points
volumes.text:
Dear Arlo, I have your brass compass still, the one you lent me in summer, and I ought to have given it back before you moved away. I did not, and I cannot post it now without a letter, and I cannot send a letter. So I am writing one for the tin in the willow instead.

Mr Greave has a map on the schoolroom wall. I measured with my thumb. Loam End is nineteen miles from Emberwick, south and a little west, past the place where the Ember goes wide.

This afternoon I stood on the bridge and tried to point your compass at you. The needle stuck at north-east, as it always does, and I had to knock it with my knuckle the way you showed me. Then it swung round and pointed down the river. I stayed until my hands were cold. Jem.

volumes.title: About the Race
volumes.text:
Dear Arlo, this is the sixth letter I have written you and hidden in the willow, and it is the one with the truth in it. That may be why I am not sending it.

You did not push off early. On your last day, when we raced the bark boats from the weir, the Otter beat my Kingfisher by the length of the mill wall, and she won fair. I had put a lead fishing weight under mine for a keel and too tall a mast, and she wallowed. I knew it when I said you cheated. I knew it when I said, good, go to Loam End then.

I was not angry about the race. I was angry that you were going on the cart the next morning, and I could not be angry at a cart. There. It is written down. Mam was half right. Jem.

volumes.title: Mending the Otter
volumes.text:
Dear Arlo, it is March. I found your boat. You moved to the Lowlands in such a hurry of boxes that you left the Otter behind, wedged in the hollow willow above the ledge where I keep these letters, which I write and do not send.

Her mast had snapped. I do not know if it was the winter or if it was like that when you put her there. I cut a hazel twig, peeled it, and whittled the foot to fit. It took three tries. Then I waxed her seams with a candle end the way your father showed us.

She is better than new and I have not sailed her. I held her over the water at the weir and could not let go. It would not be a race with one boat. She is back on her shelf in the willow, facing the door. Jem.

volumes.title: Wilf Is All Right
volumes.text:
Dear Arlo, I have to tell you something, and since these letters never get posted it is safe to tell. They sit in your old toffee tin in our willow, and you are nineteen miles off at Loam End, not reading them.

Wilf Dabb is all right. He is the marsh boy who has your desk. He can whistle through a blade of grass loud enough to turn a horse, and he knows where the eels lie up. Yesterday I showed him the weir and the stepping stones.

I did not show him the willow. He asked what was in the hollow one and I said wasps. It felt wrong all the same, standing there with him, like wearing somebody else’s coat. Then I thought, you will have a Wilf at Loam End by now, and I found I did not mind as much as I expected. Jem.

volumes.title: As Far as the Pump
volumes.text:
Dear Arlo, today I nearly sent you a letter. Not this one. This one is going in the tin in the willow, with eight others I have written since you moved to the Lowlands.

The one I nearly sent had three lines. It said: I am sorry about the race. I have your compass. I hope you are all right. I put it in my pocket and walked up Ember Street with a penny for the stamp. I got as far as the pump. The post office door was open and I could see Mrs Tansy at the scales.

Then I thought of you opening it, and reading three lines after eight months of nothing, and I turned round. I told Mam I had gone to look at the pump. She said, and how was it. I have folded the short letter inside this one. Jem.

volumes.title: News of the Heron
volumes.text:
Dear Arlo, here is the news from the weir, written in June for a tin in a willow tree, since I still have not posted you one word.

The heron we watched all last summer has a nest in the alders, and two chicks that look like angry umbrellas. The kingfisher is back on the mill post. The stepping stones are dry to their feet. Mr Greave found your initials under the desk lid at last and only said, hm. Wilf Dabb and I have begun a new dam, lower down, and it leaks.

I read the old letters through today, all nine. They are mostly news. I have been writing to you as if you were away for a week with a cold. I think I began these to say sorry, and I have said nearly everything else instead. The compass is still in my pocket. Jem.

volumes.title: Thursdays, by Loam End
volumes.text:
Dear Arlo, it is July and I found something out. I am writing it down for the tin in the willow, where I keep the letters I have not dared send you since you left Emberwick.

Mr Sedge the carrier goes through Loam End. Every other Thursday, with the Lowland parcels. I asked him this morning while he watered the horse at the pump, trying to sound as if I did not care. He said there is a lad at the mill there, thin, with a cap too big, who asks him each time whether the weir at Emberwick is still standing.

I said it was. Mr Sedge said, I know, I tell him so. Then he looked at me a while and said a parcel to Loam End costs fourpence and he leaves at eight. He did not say anything else. He did not need to. Jem.

volumes.title: The One That Goes
volumes.text:
Dear Arlo, your card came this morning. Four lines and a drawing of a boat. You wrote that you were sorry you went off without a word, and you asked if the Otter was all right. You have said sorry first. You always did win races.

So this is the letter that goes. Under it in the parcel are eleven more, September to July, that I wrote and hid in the willow. Read them in order. The early ones are the worst. Your compass is in there too, wrapped in my sock, still sticking at north-east.

The Otter is mended and she is staying here, because you will want a boat when you come at harvest. Mam says you can have the truckle bed. I am taking this to Mr Sedge now, at the pump, before eight. I am sorry about the race. You won fair. Your friend, Jem Aldery.

volumes.title: Somebody’s Spectacles
volumes.text:
To the Post Office, Emberwick. Dear Mrs Tansy, my name is Pip Hollin, I am nine, and I live at 4 Mill Row. A parcel came for me today on the carrier’s cart. It has my name on the label. It is not my parcel.

My Gran at Gullsend on the Grey Coast was sending me a blue jersey she knitted and a tin of treacle toffee. Instead there is a pair of spectacles, very strong, and a small metal whistle on a cord. I looked through the spectacles and the kitchen went like the bottom of a pond. I blew the whistle and nothing came out. Then every dog in Mill Row arrived in our yard, and is still there.

Somebody must be wanting these. I think he is old, and has a dog. Please can you find him, and my jersey. Yours truly, Philippa Hollin (Pip).

volumes.title: A Jersey for One Arm
volumes.text:
To the Postmistress at Emberwick, from Josiah Raike, shepherd, Upper Wethering in the Northern Fells. Madam, forgive the size of my writing. I make it large so that I may read it myself, my spectacles being broken these three weeks.

I sent to the spectacle-maker at Lowmarket for a new pair, and a whistle for my dog Bracken, who is going deaf to the old one. The carrier brought a parcel on Tuesday with my name on. In it is a blue jersey that would fit over one of my arms, and a tin of toffee.

I must own that I ate one piece of the toffee before I understood the parcel was not mine. I held the label to the window to be sure. It is very good toffee. Some child is going cold on my account, and I am counting sheep by guesswork. Kindly advise. J. Raike.

volumes.title: The Matter of the Ford
volumes.text:
From the Post Office, Emberwick. To Miss Pip Hollin of Mill Row and to Mr Josiah Raike of Upper Wethering, the same letter to each, since you have each other’s parcels.

I have looked into it. Last Monday the carrier’s cart crossed the ford with the river high, and two parcels took a wetting. Their labels floated off. The carrier’s lad fished them out, dried them on his knee, and pasted them back. He pasted them back the wrong way round. He is sorry, and he has been spoken to.

So, Miss Hollin, you hold a shepherd’s spectacles and dog whistle; and you, Mr Raike, a child’s jersey and toffee. Wrap them up again, please, and hand them to Barnaby Sedge the carrier on Thursday. He will bring each to its proper door. I should not blow that whistle again, Pip. W. Tansy, Postmistress.

volumes.title: Left at Reedholm
volumes.text:
Nan Fenwick, you were out at your eel traps, so I have left this under a stone on your step. It is Barnaby Sedge, the carrier. My back axle has gone on the marsh causeway and I am walking the horse home to Emberwick.

In your shed, out of the wet, are two parcels I dare not leave on the cart. They have been astray once already. One is spectacles and a dog whistle for a shepherd, Josiah Raike, up at Upper Wethering in the Fells. The other is a jersey and toffee for a child, Pip Hollin, Mill Row, Emberwick. They are labelled plain, this time by me.

If the reed-cutter goes north, give him the shepherd’s. If the punt goes down to the ferry, send the child’s by that. I shall owe you a sack of meal. Keep that goat of yours out of the shed. B. Sedge.

volumes.title: The Goat Was Thorough
volumes.text:
To the Postmistress, Emberwick, from Nan Fenwick, eel-catcher, Reedholm on the marsh. Mrs Tansy, the carrier left two parcels in my shed and a note telling me to keep the goat out. The note I found on Friday. The goat found the shed on Thursday.

Duchess has eaten both labels. She likes paste. She did not touch what was inside. I looked: spectacles and a whistle in one, a little jersey and toffee in the other. A shepherd’s and a child’s, plainly. Sedge’s note had the names, but the rain had been at it, and all I could make out was Wethering and Mill.

So I have written what I know on each in pencil. Shepherd, the Fells, went north with Dan the reed-cutter. Child, Emberwick, went down by punt to the ferry. It is the best I can do. N. Fenwick.

volumes.title: Handed Over at the Ferry
volumes.text:
To Miss Lark at the schoolhouse, Emberwick, from Corry Mott at the ferry. Miss, the marsh punt brought me a parcel this morning. All it says on it, in pencil, is Child, Emberwick. I have worked the Ember ferry thirty years, and there are a good many of those.

It is soft, and it rattles at one end like a tin of sweets. I asked the punt man who it was for. He said a goat ate the particulars. I did not ask more.

I cannot go knocking on every door in the town with a boat to mind. But every child in Emberwick passes under your eye sooner or later, so I am sending it up to you by the baker’s boy, who has promised not to shake it. Somewhere there is a small person waiting on a parcel. You will know the look. Respectfully, C. Mott.

volumes.title: Fourteen Shepherds
volumes.text:
From Mrs Hale at the Drover’s Rest, Stonecrop, to whichever shepherd this parcel belongs to. Dan the reed-cutter left it on my bar on his way north. The label says Shepherd, the Fells, in pencil, and nothing more. Fourteen shepherds drink here. I counted.

I opened it to be helpful. Spectacles and a dog whistle. On market night I set the spectacles on the bar and waited to see who squinted at them. Everybody squinted. Three tried them on. Old Tibb said they suited him, and had to be persuaded.

Then somebody remembered a man at Wethering who has been counting his flock by guesswork. So I am sending the parcel up with the parson, who walks that way on Sunday and is honest, though vague. If you are the man, there is a pint waiting here for your trouble. If you are not, pass it on. M. Hale.

volumes.title: Eleven Socks Darned
volumes.text:
To Mr Josiah Raike, Upper Wethering, from Ada Brock, Nether Wethering, at the bottom of your hill. Mr Raike, the parson left a parcel with me on Sunday. He was told Wethering and stopped at the first one he came to, as he does. It is your spectacles and a dog whistle.

I shall be honest with you. I tried the spectacles on, only to see. I have not threaded a needle at the first go in six years. That evening I threaded one straight off, and darned eleven socks, and read the back of the seed packet, and saw that the cat is not as young as I thought.

I am sending them up with my grandson this morning before I think better of it. Tell me the name of your spectacle-maker. And look in on your way down to market. Ada Brock.

volumes.title: The Lost Property Cupboard
volumes.text:
To Mrs Hollin, 4 Mill Row, from Miss Lark at the schoolhouse. Dear Mrs Hollin, Pip is bringing this note home, and a parcel with it, and I think you will want the explanation.

The ferryman sent me a parcel marked only Child, Emberwick. It spent a week in the lost property cupboard between one boot and a recorder until I remembered it on Friday. I held up what was inside before the whole school. Eleven children claimed the toffee. Only one claimed the jersey.

Pip said it was hers because the left sleeve would be longer than the right, as her Gran’s knitting always is. I measured. It is longer by a full two inches. No court could ask for better proof. She has worn it since morning lessons with the cuff turned back, and has shared the toffee fairly, by her own account. Yours, E. Lark.

volumes.title: Labels to Be Sewn
volumes.text:
To the Postmistress at Emberwick, from Mrs Dorothea Hollin, Gullsend, on the Grey Coast. Madam, my granddaughter Pip writes that the jersey I posted in October has reached her at last, by way of a ford, a shepherd, a goat, a punt and a school cupboard. I had begun to think I dreamed knitting it.

I do not blame you. I blame paste. In future I shall sew my labels on, and I advise the Board to consider it.

Pip tells me that a shepherd in the Fells, a Mr Raike, had her parcel a week, sent it back whole, and owned up to the single toffee he ate. A man like that should not go without a jersey of his own. Kindly ask him his chest measure and the length of his arm. Both arms, tell him. I shall do my best about the sleeves. D. Hollin.

volumes.title: A Twist of Fell Wool
volumes.text:
To Miss Pip Hollin, Mill Row, Emberwick, from Josiah Raike, shepherd, Upper Wethering. Miss Hollin, you will see my writing has shrunk. My spectacles came up the hill on Monday with a small boy, six weeks late. I counted the flock that same hour. I had guessed two hundred and four. There are two hundred and six, and I have apologised to the pair of them.

The whistle works. Bracken heard it from the far side of the tarn and came like a thrown stone. I am told the dogs of Mill Row can vouch for it.

I had your jersey a week and one of your toffees for good. To square the account I enclose a twist of wool from my best ewe, for your grandmother. She has sent to ask the length of my arms. I have never been so measured. Your friend, J. Raike.

volumes.title: No Labels This Time
volumes.text:
To Mr Josiah Raike, shepherd, Upper Wethering. Dear Mr Raike, thank you for the wool. Gran says it is the best she ever had and she is knitting your jersey out of it, grey, with a blue band from what was left of mine. So we will match a bit.

I am wearing my jersey now. The left sleeve is too long, the same as always. I am glad you ate a toffee. It means you know what they are like. I have saved you two more.

Gran is coming at shearing time, and we are all riding up on Mr Sedge’s cart to bring your jersey ourselves. Nobody is posting it. Mrs Tansy says that is a slight on the service and very wise. Please tell Bracken I shall bring her a bone. The dogs of Mill Row still look at me hopefully. Your friend, Pip Hollin.

volumes.title: Arrived, Sea Present
volumes.text:
Maud. Arrived at Cockleby four o’clock, train only nine minutes late, sandwiches eaten by Lowmarket. The sea is here. It is a good deal larger than the picture on the chapel raffle ticket led me to expect, and it does not keep still. They call this the Grey Coast, but I should say pewter, with a polish on it.

Mrs Crabb’s boarding house is called Sea View. There is one, if I stand on the bed. Supper was a kipper. You said when I left that I should not put so much as a toe in the water, and that forty years behind a button counter had made me unfit for holidays. I have twelve days to prove you wrong and I have brought the stout shoes. Do not let Mrs Peabody have thread on account. Effie.

volumes.title: The Promenade, Twice
volumes.text:
Maud. Day two at Cockleby. Walked the promenade end to end, twice, to get my bearings. It has forty-one benches, a bandstand with no band, and a man who sells cockles from a barrow and calls everybody captain. I was captain twice.

Sat a full hour looking at the sea, which is longer than I have sat looking at anything since the shop opened. The tide went out while I watched. Nobody stopped it. There is a boy called Dob on the sands with a donkey named Admiral, a penny a ride; I declined, with thanks, and Admiral looked relieved.

Toe not yet in. I walked down to where the wet sand begins and a wave came at my shoes, so I came back. I am studying the enemy. The grey darning wool, if anyone asks, is behind the hooks and eyes. Effie.

volumes.title: One Toe, Witnessed
volumes.text:
Maud. The toe is in. Left foot, big one, seven o’clock this morning, before anyone was about to see my ankles. The sea at Cockleby is as cold as the pump handle in January. I said a word I shall not write on a postcard that the postman may read.

I was seen, however. Four ladies came down the beach in bathing dresses and went straight in up to the neck, talking the whole while about marmalade. The stoutest, a Mrs Orla Finn, called out, well done, that is how it starts. They swim every morning and go home to one teapot between them, so they call themselves the Early Kettles.

She has asked me to come again tomorrow. I said I would think about it. I have thought. You owe me an apology regarding toes, and may send it by return. Effie.

volumes.title: Rain and the Shell Museum
volumes.text:
Maud. Rained all day at Cockleby, sideways. Mrs Crabb says it does that. No sea for me, so I went to the Shell Museum, which is one room over the chandler’s, kept by a retired harbourmaster who takes twopence and follows you round.

Four hundred shells in trays, Maud, every one labelled in a hand as neat as yours. Some no bigger than a shirt button and some you could bath a baby in. He showed me how mother-of-pearl is cut. I told him I had sold pearl buttons for forty years and never once thought of them having lived in the sea. He was very much shocked.

I have bought two dozen pearl buttons for the shop, at trade, after some discussion. They are in my stocking drawer. We shall put them in the window when I am home and say they are from the coast. Effie.

volumes.title: Up to the Knees
volumes.text:
Maud. Day five at the coast and I have been in to the knees. Mrs Finn of the Early Kettles, the ladies who swim before breakfast, lent me a bathing dress. It is navy serge and has more cloth in it than my winter coat. I changed in a hut that smelt of wet rope.

The trick, they tell me, is not to stop and consider. I stopped and considered for some minutes. Then a small wave settled the matter by coming to me. Knees, Maud, both of them, in the open sea. The sand moves under your feet as if someone were pulling a rug gently.

Afterwards, tea from their one teapot and a ginger biscuit. I could not feel my feet until half past nine and did not mind. If the traveller in ribbons calls, do not let him sell you the mauve. Effie.

volumes.title: The Hat Departs
volumes.text:
Maud. Bad news, and you are to bear it calmly. My good straw hat is gone, the one with the cherries. I walked to the end of the pier at Cockleby this afternoon to see the boats, the wind came round the lamp post without any warning, and off it went.

It did not fall in the sea at once. It bowled along the pier like a hoop, hopped the rail, and flew, Maud, a good deal better than it ever sat. I last saw it heading for the lighthouse with a gull in attendance. A gentleman offered to run after it, but there was only water to run on.

Eleven years I had that hat. I am wearing a headscarf of Mrs Crabb’s with anchors on it and feel like a fishwife, though a cheerful one. No bathing today on account of the wind. Six days left. Effie.

volumes.title: Admiral Finds a Hat
volumes.text:
Maud. The hat is found. It blew off the pier yesterday, you recall. This morning the boy Dob came to the door of my boarding house leading his donkey, Admiral, with my straw hat on the donkey’s head, one ear through the brim.

They found it on the sands at low tide, a mile along, sitting on a rock as if waiting for a cab. It is salt-stained, and the cherries are gone. Dob says the gull had them. I looked at Admiral, and Admiral looked at the sea, and I have my own opinion.

I gave the boy sixpence and the donkey a carrot, which was generous in the circumstances. Then I had a penny ride after all, Maud, to the breakwater and back, holding on with both hands. As for the hat, it has seen more of the coast than I have. Effie.

volumes.title: Waist Deep, Maud
volumes.text:
Maud. Waist deep. I write it large so the postman may know too. Eight days at Cockleby and I have stood in the Grey Coast sea up to the buttons of a borrowed bathing dress, with the Early Kettles round me in a ring like hens round a new pullet.

A wave took a liberty and went over my shoulder. I shrieked. I have not shrieked since the mouse in the ribbon drawer, and that was nothing like so pleasant. Mrs Finn says tomorrow I am to lie back and let the water hold me. I said the water and I had not been introduced long enough.

Tea from the one teapot afterwards, and I was given the cup without the chip, which I understand is an honour. Your card came. I accept the apology about the toe, though it was grudging. The mauve ribbon will never sell. Effie.

volumes.title: Fish Supper on the Wall
volumes.text:
Maud. No bathing today, it being Sunday. Instead I must confess that I ate my supper in the street. Fried fish, out of a paper, with my fingers, sitting on the harbour wall at Cockleby with my feet hanging over. You are not to tell the chapel.

The boats came in while I ate. Seven of them, with brown sails, one behind another round the lighthouse, and the women went down with baskets to meet them. A man threw a rope and a boy caught it without looking. Then the lamps were lit along the quay and came out again upside down in the water.

I sat till my paper was empty and the gulls gave me up. Forty years I have shut the shop at six and gone in to a boiled egg. I did not know evenings came in this size. Three days left. Effie.

volumes.title: Floating, After a Fashion
volumes.text:
Maud. I have floated. Mrs Finn of the Early Kettles stood behind me in the sea at Cockleby this morning with a hand under each shoulder and said, lie back, Miss Brindle, as if into a chair. I said there was no chair. She said that was rather the point.

So I lay back. My feet came up by themselves, which nobody had warned me of, and there was nothing to look at but sky. One gull. A small cloud shaped like the iron. The water held me as a counter holds a bolt of cloth, without comment. Then she took her hands away and I floated alone for a count of three before I remembered myself and sank.

Three seconds, Maud. I am fifty-eight and I did not know I could be carried. Two days left. I have asked what comes after floating. They say strokes. Effie.

volumes.title: Six Strokes Counted
volumes.text:
Maud. I have swum. Six strokes, counted aloud by four witnesses, along the beach at Cockleby and not out of my depth, since I am not a fool. It was not elegant. Mrs Finn says I swim like a person beating a carpet. But I began in one place and finished in another with no foot on the bottom, and that is swimming.

I swallowed some sea on the fourth stroke. It tastes exactly as you would suppose. The Early Kettles, my bathing ladies, gave three cheers, and the cockle man on the promenade took off his cap, though he may only have been scratching.

Eight days ago I put in one toe and thought myself brave. Tell nobody at home; I wish to mention it myself, in passing, at the chapel tea, and watch Mrs Peabody’s face. Home the day after tomorrow. Air my bed. Effie.

volumes.title: Home Tomorrow, Maud
volumes.text:
Maud. Last card from Cockleby. I come home tomorrow by the train that gets in at twenty to six. My box is packed: one straw hat without cherries, two dozen pearl buttons, a paper of shrimps for your tea, and a stoppered jar of the sea, so that you may put your own toe in and tell me how you like it.

I swam ten strokes this morning for a farewell. The Early Kettles gave me the unchipped cup again and a ginger biscuit for the train. Dob brought Admiral to the door of Sea View to say goodbye. I shook hands with one of them.

Now attend. I have paid Mrs Crabb a deposit on two beds for the first fortnight of next June. Two, Maud. The shop can wear a card in the door for once. Bring stout shoes. Put the kettle on at six. Effie.
